source.title: Toy Models of Superposition
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Nicholas Schiefer; T. Henighan; S. Kravec; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; R. Lasenby; Dawn Drain; Carol Chen; R. Grosse; Sam McCandlish; J. Kaplan; D. Amodei; M. Wattenberg; Chris Olah

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and figures are flattened or omitted in the web text, but the document is identifiable and its main results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: This is the original study, not a reproduction. It directly tests toy-model superposition with trained synthetic-feature networks; T2 is the closest tranche category available.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own toy-model experiments and reported outcomes. The paper also mentions empirical observations and results from other work on LLMs and vision models; those are cited or described as prior observations, not new results from this study, and are not rows. Values visible only in figures are not transcribed as numbers.
record.test_reason: This is the original source of V1 and V2. It trains toy ReLU networks on synthetic sparse features and reports superposition, its sparsity- and importance-dependent phase changes, polytope geometry, and neurons that are polysemantic because of superposition. No tranche category exists for 'original', so T1 (the defining method and measure) is used. Per the rules, no verdict labels are given because the study is the version's original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the following points. The authors claim a direct demonstration that superposition occurs in toy networks and fully explains polysemanticity there. Superposition is governed by a phase change in sparsity and importance. Computation (absolute value) can be done in superposition. They judge that superposition, the mono/polysemantic neuron mix, and perhaps the adversarial link are likely to generalize to real networks, while the geometry and learning-dynamics results are much more uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: This is the original study. It trains small ReLU networks on synthetic sparse features and examines learned feature directions, overlap, and geometry; there is no prior recipe being reproduced here.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome changes with feature sparsity, relative feature importance, feature correlations, and the activation-function/model setup. Optimization and selecting the lowest-loss fit also affect the displayed results in some experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial vulnerability rises sharply (>3x) as superposition forms and tracks features per dimension. Adversarial training reduces superposition but needs ~80% input-norm attacks to eliminate it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy ReLU output models, superposition increases vulnerability to L2 adversarial attacks, and adversarial training can reduce superposition at high attack strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Asymmetric superposition plus inhibition motif used to compute absolute value in superposition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy networks can perform nonlinear computation on superposed features via specific weight motifs.

record.problems: Evidence is from synthetic toy networks rather than real models. Many outcomes are described qualitatively, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The ReLU hidden-layer identity model can evade its nonlinearity, and some visualized results select the lowest-loss fit from many trainings. The authors also report optimization difficulties for some geometries and explicitly caution that geometry and learning-dynamics results may be idiosyncratic.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible findings omitted. Discussion of LLMs, InceptionV1, prior interpretability studies, and external replication statements are not new results from this study's own experiments.

untested.parts: Generalization beyond toy autoencoder/absolute-value models. The authors flag geometry results as possibly idiosyncratic to the toy model.
Whether capacity pressure explains polysemanticity in real networks. InceptionV1 and transformer MLP observations are cited or anecdotal, not new measurements.
No experiment. Related Work only argues a maximally distributed code can be polysemantic without superposition.
No LLM measurements or dictionary recovery. Sparse coding is discussed only as a proposed strategy.
Not tested; SAEs postdate the study.
Assumes linear 1-D feature directions. The multidimensional-features appendix is referenced but not in the text. The nonlinear compression appendix is a constructed example, not a test.

missing.what: Learning dynamics: features jump between discrete dimensionalities with sudden loss drops. Learning for 6 features in m=3 proceeds through distinct geometric transformations ending in an octahedron.
missing.locator: Superposition and Learning Dynamics — Phenomena 1 and 2

missing.what: Linear vs ReLU hidden-layer model comparison: with the ReLU hidden layer, features align with neurons and many neurons are dedicated to one feature.
missing.locator: Superposition in a Privileged Basis (intro comparison figure)

missing.what: Primary/secondary feature neurons: large weight for one feature, smaller weights for others, in the absolute-value model.
missing.locator: Computation in Superposition — Superposition vs Sparsity

record.verdict_notes: This is the original source for V1 and V2, so no labels are assigned. The reader's tranche T2 is changed to T1. Independent replications (Redwood, DeepMind, OpenAI) are reported in the comments section. They are not this study's results, but note them: Redwood found the phase diagrams depend on the activation function, and McGrath found a 'confused feature' phase. Rows R1–R13 are well-formed, though most are qualitative, read from figures, with no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether the toy-model findings hold in real LLMs or other real networks.
Tests toy-model feature importance and polysemantic neurons, but not whether capacity pressure is the cause of polysemanticity in real networks.
Does not test polysemanticity arising through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Does not measure feature spread or recover sparse features in LLMs; its discussion of real models refers to prior work or author experience.
Does not test whether SAE or other dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical.
Uses feature directions in its toy-model setup but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: linear model
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned feature representations across sparsity levels
rows.measure: Number and geometry of represented features
rows.value: The model always learns the top-m most important features, analogous to top principal components.
rows.note: The paper reports this as the linear-model comparison: it does not represent extra features in superposition.
rows.check: State is correct: the linear model is a no-superposition comparator. Its role is a control, not a test of V1 in its target system (nonlinear small networks).

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.size_stated: n = 20 features; m = 5 hidden dimensions; I_i = 0.7^i
rows.operation_detail: Measured learned feature vectors and their overlap across sparsity levels
rows.measure: Number of represented features and non-orthogonality
rows.baseline: Linear model represents the top-m features
rows.value: Matches the linear-model behavior on dense features; as sparsity increases, the model represents more features non-orthogonally, initially using antipodal pairs and then other geometries.
rows.note: The text describes the sweep qualitatively; it does not give individual sparsity values or row-wise numerical outcomes.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.size_stated: n = 80 features; m = 20 hidden dimensions; I_i = 0.9^i
rows.operation_detail: Visualized feature representation in a larger model
rows.value: The results are described as essentially a rescaled version of the smaller-model visualization.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative result, not individual values from the visualization.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Swept the extra feature's importance and feature sparsity; compared not learned, superposed, and orthogonally represented outcomes
rows.measure: Optimal encoding of the extra feature
rows.baseline: Compared configurations include ignoring the extra feature, dedicating the dimension to it, or encoding both features antipodally
rows.value: The paper reports an empirical and theoretical phase change: sparsity is necessary for superposition, and the encoding strategy also varies with relative feature importance.
rows.note: The paper calls the empirical change discontinuous in magnitude and superposition; specific boundary values are not stated.

source_check.locator_found: Superposition as a Phase Change, lines 630–663.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Varied the extra feature's relative importance and sparsity and examined encoding strategies
rows.measure: Which feature is ignored, dedicated, or put in an antipodal pair
rows.baseline: Theoretical configurations considered include ignoring the extra feature, ignoring one of the other features, or using antipodal pairs
rows.value: The diagrams are reported to suggest phase changes between feature-encoding strategies.
rows.note: The paper says the theoretical comparison does not include the configuration putting all three features into joint superposition.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Swept feature sparsity and measured dimensions per represented feature
rows.measure: D* = m / ||W||²_F, interpreted as dimensions per feature
rows.value: The curve is described as having sticky points at 1 and 1/2; the 1/2 regime corresponds to antipodal pairs, with two features per hidden dimension.
rows.locator: The Geometry of Superposition — Uniform Superposition
rows.note: The authors say feature count and hidden dimension do not matter much when n is much larger than m, and that doubling m doubles the number of learned features.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-feature dimensionality and inspected feature-vector geometry
rows.baseline: 0 denotes a feature not learned; 1 denotes a dedicated dimension
rows.value: Reported clusters at dimensionalities 3/4 (tetrahedron), 2/3 (triangle), 1/2 (antipodal pair), 2/5 (pentagon), and 3/8 (square antiprism).
rows.locator: The Geometry of Superposition — Feature Dimensionality; Why These Geometric Structures?
rows.note: The paper interprets the fractions as corresponding to specific feature-vector geometries.

source_check.locator_found: Uniform Superposition; Feature Dimensionality; Why These Geometric Structures?, lines 695–801.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Changed the sparsity of one feature while leaving other features uniform

conditions.value: one feature made more or less sparse

rows.measure: Feature geometry and whether the varied feature is represented
rows.baseline: Uniform case gives a regular pentagon
rows.value: Changing sparsity deforms the pentagon; making the feature sufficiently sparse produces a phase change to two digons, with the varied feature at zero.
rows.locator: The Geometry of Superposition — Non-Uniform Superposition, Perturbing a Single Feature
rows.note: The paper reports that the geometry changes smoothly before the phase change.

source_check.locator_found: Non-Uniform Superposition — Perturbing a Single Feature, lines 879–906.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Varied sparsity of paired features that activate together

conditions.value: features in each pair always activate together; their non-zero values are uncorrelated

rows.value: In the very sparse regime, features form a hexagon with correlated features side-by-side; as sparsity decreases, pairs progressively collapse into their principal components, and the dense solution becomes equivalent to PCA.
rows.locator: The Geometry of Superposition — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features, Collapsing of Correlated Features
rows.note: The authors characterize superposition and PCA as strategies that trade off as sparsity and correlation change.

rows.subject: larger toy model
rows.operation_detail: Visualized WᵀW for two sets of correlated features

conditions.value: two sets of co-occurring correlated features

rows.value: The authors report a local almost-orthogonal basis: correlated feature sets considered in isolation are nearly orthogonal, despite the model overall being in superposition.
rows.locator: The Geometry of Superposition — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features, Local Almost-Orthogonal Bases
rows.note: The paper presents this as a possible local non-superposition property, not a general property of the full representation.

rows.subject: small toy models
rows.operation_detail: Compared organization of correlated and anticorrelated feature sets

conditions.value: correlated sets activate together; anticorrelated sets allow only one feature in a set to be active at a time

rows.value: Correlated features are reported to prefer orthogonal directions, then proximity when orthogonality fails, and principal-component collapse when capacity is insufficient; anticorrelated features prefer interference, especially negative interference.
rows.locator: The Geometry of Superposition — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features
rows.note: The passage summarizes the reported preferences across experiments; it does not give numerical effect sizes.

rows.subject: ReLU hidden layer toy model
rows.operation_detail: Visualized weights and neuron feature mixtures across sparsity levels; selected the lowest-loss model
rows.measure: Monosemantic versus polysemantic neurons and feature-to-neuron alignment
rows.value: Monosemantic neurons occur in some sparsity regimes and polysemantic neurons in others; both can occur in the same model. Polysemantic solutions are described as structured and neuron-aligned.
rows.locator: Superposition in a Privileged Basis — Visualizing Superposition in Terms of Neurons
rows.note: The authors note that this model can circumvent its hidden-layer ReLU and describe this as a limitation.

rows.subject: absolute-value ReLU hidden layer toy model
rows.operation_detail: Trained the model to compute absolute value while varying feature sparsity
rows.measure: Feature mixtures in neurons while computing the target
rows.baseline: In the dense regime, each neuron represents a single feature
rows.value: At sufficient sparsity, the model uses superposition to represent more features than neurons and still usefully approximates the computation. In intermediate regimes, some neurons are pure while a subset are highly polysemantic; neurons representing the most important features tend to be monosemantic.
rows.locator: Computation in Superposition — Superposition vs Sparsity
rows.note: The paper states that losses across sparsity levels are not directly comparable because they measure different tasks.

rows.subject: ReLU output toy model
rows.operation_detail: Applied analytically derived L2 adversarial attacks

conditions.value: maximum L2 norm 0.1 of average input norm

rows.baseline: Vulnerability before superposition forms; exact value not stated
rows.value: Vulnerability sharply increases as superposition forms, by >3x, and closely tracks features per dimension.
rows.note: This measures an effect associated with superposition, not one of the behaviors named in V1–V6.

rows.subject: ReLU output toy model
rows.operation_detail: Used adversarial training with the analytic optimal attack against a random feature
rows.value: Adversarial training reduced superposition; attacks had to be unreasonably large (80% input L2 norm) to eliminate it fully.
rows.note: The authors say they did not explore the result further and that stronger attacks might work better.
rows.check: Adversarial training is an intervention that reduces superposition. It does not measure whether superposition arises with sparsity or with regular geometry, so it does not bear on V1. It belongs with R14 under fits_no_version. The 'partial' state is not meaningful against V1.

rows.subject: absolute-value ReLU hidden layer toy model
rows.operation_detail: Compared the learned computation with the non-superposed absolute-value construction
rows.measure: Hidden-neuron representation used for the computation
rows.baseline: Without superposition, two hidden neurons are needed per feature
rows.value: The model computes absolute value with a positive-side and a negative-side neuron for each input feature, as expected without superposition.
rows.note: This is the small-model non-superposition comparison; the paper notes a weight-rescaling freedom.
rows.check: With n=3 features and m=6 neurons there is no capacity pressure (2 neurons are needed per feature), so absence of superposition is the expected control, not a failure of V1.

relation.reason: Its experiments directly measure superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, feature allocation, and geometry in toy networks.

tranche.reason: This original study establishes the reference method and measures; T1 is consistent with that recipe, although it is not a replication.

source_check.notes: Original-source results receive no verdicts under the rules. The authors explicitly leave generalization to real networks uncertain, especially geometry and learning dynamics; checks of ellipsized row fields cover their visible content.
